# Background

# Data

## Loading the Data

```{r libraries}
library(sf)
library(tmap)
library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)
```

```{r}
nc_tracts <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = c(
    educational.health.care.count = "B08126_011",
    male.age.65.to.66 = "B01001_020",
    male.age.67.to.69 = "B01001_021",
    male.age.70.to.74 = "B01001_022",
    male.age.75.to.79 = "B01001_023",
    male.age.80.to.84 = "B01001_024",
    male.age.85.over = "B01001_025",
    female.age.65.to.66 = "B01001_044",
    female.age.67.to.69 = "B01001_045",
    female.age.70.to.74 = "B01001_046",
    female.age.75.to.79 = "B01001_047",
    female.age.80.to.84 = "B01001_048",
    female.age.85.over = "B01001_049",
    median.home.value = "B25077_001",
    year.of.home = "B25035_001",
    undergrad = "B14001_008"
  ),
  state = "NC",
  year = 2020,
  output = "wide",
  geometry = TRUE
)
```

I am using 2020 Census data to examine North Carolina at both the county
and census tract levels. Comparing these two geographic scales will help
show whether the relationships between the variables change depending on
the size of the area being studied.

```{r}
nc_county <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
```

# Methods

> To prepare the data for the regression models, I calculated the
> elderly population by adding together the number of men and women aged
> 65 and older. I did this for both census tracts and counties so I
> could compare the results at different geographic scales.

```{r}
nc_tracts <- nc_tracts |>
  mutate(
    elderly = male.age.65.to.66E +
      male.age.67.to.69E +
      male.age.70.to.74E +
      male.age.75.to.79E +
      male.age.80.to.84E +
      male.age.85.overE +
      female.age.65.to.66E +
      female.age.67.to.69E +
      female.age.70.to.74E +
      female.age.75.to.79E +
      female.age.80.to.84E +
      female.age.85.overE
  )

nc_county <- nc_county |>
  mutate(
    elderly = male.age.65.to.66E +
      male.age.67.to.69E +
      male.age.70.to.74E +
      male.age.75.to.79E +
      male.age.80.to.84E +
      male.age.85.overE +
      female.age.65.to.66E +
      female.age.67.to.69E +
      female.age.70.to.74E +
      female.age.75.to.79E +
      female.age.80.to.84E +
      female.age.85.overE
  )
```

> Some census tracts have missing information for median home value or
> the year homes were built. I removed these observations so they would
> not interfere with the regression analysis.

```{r}
nc_tracts <- nc_tracts |>
  drop_na(median.home.valueE, year.of.homeE) |>
  filter(year.of.homeE > 1000)
```

### First Model: Elderly Population and Education/Healthcare Employment

```{r}
first.model.tract <- lm(
  educational.health.care.countE ~ elderly,
  data = nc_tracts
)

summary(first.model.tract)
```

The results show a positive relationship between the elderly population
and the number of educational and healthcare workers at the census tract
level. The elderly variable has a coefficient of 0.242, meaning that
each additional elderly resident is associated with approximately 0.24
more workers. Both the elderly variable and the overall model have
p-values below 0.05, making them statistically significant. However, the
adjusted R-squared is 0.1233, meaning the model only explains about
12.3% of the variation in educational and healthcare workers. This
suggests that other factors may also influence employment in these
fields.

`### County-Level Regression`

```{r}
first.model.county <- lm(
  educational.health.care.countE ~ elderly,
  data = nc_county
)

summary(first.model.county)
```

At the county level, the results show a strong positive relationship
between the elderly population and the number of educational and
healthcare workers. The coefficient for elderly is 0.8417, meaning that
each additional elderly resident is associated with approximately 0.84
more workers. Both the elderly variable and the overall model have
p-values below 0.05, showing that the relationship is statistically
significant. The adjusted R-squared is 0.93, meaning the model explains
about 93% of the variation in educational and healthcare workers across
counties. This is much higher than the 12.3% explained at the census
tract level, suggesting that the relationship appears much stronger when
the data is analyzed at a larger geographic scale.

### Graphing the Variables

```{r}
ggplot(nc_tracts, aes(
  x = elderly,
  y = educational.health.care.countE
)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "blue") +
  labs(
    title = "Elderly Population and Education/Healthcare Workers",
    subtitle = "North Carolina Census Tracts, 2020",
    x = "Population Aged 65+",
    y = "Education and Healthcare Workers"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
ggplot(nc_county, aes(
  x = elderly,
  y = educational.health.care.countE
)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "blue") +
  labs(
    title = "Elderly Population and Education/Healthcare Workers",
    subtitle = "North Carolina Counties, 2020",
    x = "Population Aged 65+",
    y = "Education and Healthcare Workers"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

When comparing the two graphs, I noticed that the relationship between
the elderly population and education and healthcare employment is much
stronger at the county level. The county-level graph shows that most
points follow the regression line fairly closely, while the census tract
graph has more scattered points. This matches the adjusted R-squared
values, which were 0.93 for counties and 0.1233 for census tracts. One
possible reason for this difference is that counties cover larger
populations, so the relationship between the two variables becomes more
noticeable when the data is grouped into larger geographic areas.

### Mapping Regression Residuals

```{r}
nc_tracts$residuals <- NA_real_

used_rows <- as.integer(
  rownames(model.frame(first.model.tract))
)

nc_tracts$residuals[used_rows] <-
  residuals(first.model.tract)

# Map the residuals
ggplot(nc_tracts) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = residuals), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "blue",
    mid = "white",
    high = "red",
    midpoint = 0,
    na.value = "grey90"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Regression Residuals by Census Tract",
    subtitle = "North Carolina, 2020",
    fill = "Residual"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The residual map shows how the model's predictions differ from the
actual number of education and healthcare workers across North Carolina
census tracts. The red areas represent places where the model
underestimated the number of workers, while the purple areas represent
places where it overestimated them. I noticed that some of the larger
positive residuals appear in central North Carolina, while negative
residuals are spread across several parts of the state. This suggests
that the relationship between elderly population and employment is not
the same everywhere, and other local factors may help explain the
differences.

### County level Residual Map

```{r}
nc_county$residuals <- residuals(first.model.county)

ggplot(nc_county) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = residuals), color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "blue",
    mid = "white",
    high = "red",
    midpoint = 0
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Regression Residuals by County",
    subtitle = "North Carolina, 2020",
    fill = "Residual"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The county-level residual map shows that the model does not predict
education and healthcare employment equally well across North Carolina.
Some counties in the north-central part of the state have positive
residuals, meaning they have more workers than the model predicted.
There is also a county in southeastern North Carolina with a large
negative residual, meaning the model predicted more workers than were
actually reported. Although the county-level regression had a high
adjusted R-squared of 0.93, these differences show that the model still
makes errors in certain areas. This suggests that other factors besides
the elderly population may help explain employment patterns.

## Second Model: Multiple Regressions

For my second model, I wanted to see whether adding more variables would
help explain the number of education and healthcare workers in North
Carolina. Along with the elderly population, I included undergraduate
enrollment and median home value to see whether these factors were also
associated with employment in these fields.

```{r}
second.model.tract <- lm(
  educational.health.care.countE ~ elderly +
    undergradE + median.home.valueE,
  data = nc_tracts
)

summary(second.model.tract)
```

For my second regression model, I included elderly population,
undergraduate enrollment, and median home value to see whether these
variables were related to education and healthcare employment. All three
variables had positive coefficients and p-values below 0.05, meaning
they were statistically significant. The elderly population had a
coefficient of 0.2435, while undergraduate enrollment had a coefficient
of 0.2042. Median home value also had a positive coefficient, although
its effect per dollar was much smaller. The adjusted R-squared was
0.2315, meaning the model explained about 23.15% of the variation in
employment. This was an improvement from the first model, which only
explained 12.33%.

```{r}
nc_tracts$second_residuals <- NA_real_

used_rows <- as.integer(
  rownames(model.frame(second.model.tract))
)

nc_tracts$second_residuals[used_rows] <-
  residuals(second.model.tract)

# Create residual map
ggplot(nc_tracts) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = second_residuals), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "blue",
    mid = "white",
    high = "red",
    midpoint = 0,
    na.value = "grey90"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Residuals from the Multiple Regression Model",
    subtitle = "North Carolina Census Tracts, 2020",
    fill = "Residual"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The residual map for my second model shows that there are still
differences between the predicted and actual number of education and
healthcare workers across North Carolina. Some areas have positive
residuals, while others have negative residuals, meaning the model
underestimates employment in some places and overestimates it in others.
Compared to the first model, the second model explains more variation
because it includes additional variables like undergraduate enrollment
and median home value. However, the residuals show that there are still
other factors affecting employment that the model does not account for.

# Results

Overall, my results show that elderly population has a positive
relationship with education and healthcare employment in North Carolina.
The first regression model had an adjusted R-squared of 0.1233 at the
census tract level, compared to 0.93 at the county level. This suggests
that the relationship is much stronger when looking at larger geographic
areas. My second model included undergraduate enrollment and median home
value, which increased the adjusted R-squared to 0.2315 at the census
tract level. All three variables were statistically significant, but the
residual maps showed that the models still had prediction errors in
different parts of the state.

# Conclusion

This analysis helped me understand how linear regression can be used to
examine relationships between demographic characteristics and
employment. I found that elderly population was positively associated
with education and healthcare employment, especially at the county
level. Adding undergraduate enrollment and median home value improved
the census tract model, but it still did not explain all of the
variation. One limitation is that counties with larger populations
naturally tend to have more elderly residents and workers, which may
affect the results. Overall, this assignment showed me that both the
variables included in a model and the geographic scale of the analysis
can influence the results.
